verses.text: After this, Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar; and Amnon the son of David loved her.
Amnon was so troubled that he became sick because of his sister Tamar; for she was a virgin; and it seemed hard to Amnon to do anything to her.
But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David’s brother; and Jonadab was a very subtle man.
He said to him, “Why, son of the king, are you so sad from day to day? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lay down on your bed, and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, tell him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it, and eat it from her hand.’”

So Amnon lay down and faked being sick. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, “Please let my sister Tamar come, and make me a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand.”
Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, “Go now to your brother Amnon’s house, and prepare food for him.”
So Tamar went to her brother Amnon’s house; and he was lying down. She took dough, and kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked the cakes.
She took the pan, and poured them out before him; but he refused to eat. Amnon said, “Have all men leave me.” Then every man went out from him.
Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the room, that I may eat from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes which she had made, and brought them into the room to Amnon her brother.
When she had brought them near to him to eat, he took hold of her, and said to her, “Come, lie with me, my sister!”
She answered him, “No, my brother, do not force me! For no such thing ought to be done in Israel. Don’t you do this folly.
As for me, where would I carry my shame? And as for you, you will be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king; for he will not withhold me from you.”
However he would not listen to her voice; but being stronger than she, he forced her, and lay with her.
Then Amnon hated her with exceedingly great hatred; for the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Amnon said to her, “Arise, be gone!”
She said to him, “Not so, because this great wrong in sending me away is worse than the other that you did to me!” But he would not listen to her.
Then he called his servant who ministered to him, and said, “Now put this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her.”
She had a garment of various colors on her; for the king’s daughters who were virgins dressed in such robes. Then his servant brought her out and bolted the door after her.
Tamar put ashes on her head, and tore her garment of various colors that was on her; and she laid her hand on her head, and went her way, crying aloud as she went.

Absalom her brother said to her, “Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take this thing to heart.” So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom’s house.
But when king David heard of all these things, he was very angry.
Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.
After two full years, Absalom had sheep shearers in Baal Hazor, which is beside Ephraim: and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
Absalom came to the king, and said, “See now, your servant has sheep shearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant.”
The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you.” He pressed him; however he would not go, but blessed him.
Then Absalom said, “If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us.” The king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom pressed him, and he let Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.

Absalom commanded his servants, saying, “Mark now, when Amnon’s heart is merry with wine; and when I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then kill him. Don’t be afraid. Haven’t I commanded you? Be courageous, and be valiant!”
The servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king’s sons arose, and every man got up on his mule, and fled.
While they were on the way, the news came to David, saying, “Absalom has slain all the king’s sons, and there is not one of them left!”
Then the king arose, and tore his garments, and lay on the earth; and all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David’s brother, answered, “Don’t let my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men the king’s sons; for Amnon only is dead; for by the appointment of Absalom this has been determined from the day that he forced his sister Tamar.
Now therefore don’t let my lord the king take the thing to his heart, to think that all the king’s sons are dead; for only Amnon is dead.”
But Absalom fled. The young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold, many people were coming by way of the hillside behind him.
Jonadab said to the king, “Behold, the king’s sons are coming! It is as your servant said.”
As soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king’s sons came, and lifted up their voice, and wept. The king also and all his servants wept bitterly.
But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai the son of Ammihur, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day.
So Absalom fled, and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
King David longed to go out to Absalom; for he was comforted concerning Amnon, since he was dead.

footnotes.content: A beautiful sister, a secret love that becomes obsession. I've seen how desire left unchecked can twist the heart—what starts as attraction becomes a sickness, and pride refuses to look away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amnon is sick with lust, paralyzed by it. But notice—his sickness comes from his own heart, not from Tamar's beauty. There's always a moment when we can turn from the bent desire; he chooses not to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonadab is subtle—a counselor to schemes, not to righteousness. I've learned that subtle evil often wears a friendly face and promises to solve what only God can heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amnon confesses his desire to a friend, and the friend hears a problem to solve, not a sin to resist. How easily we find ears that will listen to our excuses instead of our repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the wicked counsel: a simple lie, a pretense of sickness. Notice how the trap is laid—Jonadab knows exactly how to use David's gentleness and Tamar's obedience against them both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lie becomes Amnon's own words to David, his own request to the king. When we rehearse a sin, even in speaking it out, we make it more real, not less.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David, trusting his son, sends Tamar to serve her brother—an act of love that the wicked have set up for ruin. Even a king's good judgment can be used by those who mean evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar goes, caring for her brother, and does her kindness with her own hands. She is innocent and willing, which makes what follows even more terrible—and his wickedness even more plain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He refuses the food she has made and orders everyone to leave. The lie is complete now—sickness forgotten, the moment stripped of all pretense. Wickedness always strips away pretense in the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He draws her into the inner room, deeper into isolation. I've learned that sin isolates us from witnesses, from help, from the light of others' presence—this is the very shape of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the true nature of his 'love' is revealed—it was never love at all, but appetite clothed in longing. The first real act of this love is force, not tenderness. What a terrible unmasking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar speaks sense—she refuses, appeals to the law, even offers what she thinks might spare her. But when a man has chosen force, words cannot reach him. She does what she can; the blame is his alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She names the shame he brings on her, appeals to his own reputation. Even in terror, she tries reason—but she cannot reach a heart set on violence. Her innocence makes his guilt only darker.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He forces her. The verse is plain, and so is the weight—he chose strength over mercy, appetite over kindness, and in that moment tore not just her body but her whole future.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now his 'love' turns to hatred—greater even than the love that came before. This is what lust always becomes when it has taken what it wanted: contempt, disgust at itself and its object.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar pleads not to be cast out—in her moment, she cannot see that his presence is the wound, his house the place of her ruin. The cruelty of his rejection compounds the crime.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He calls his servant to throw her out, bolt the door. The same man he ordered to leave now helps him erase her, as though she were never there—but the Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The garment of many colors marked her as the king's daughter, a virgin of the royal house—a visible sign of her dignity and protection. Cast out in it, she becomes a living sign of the violated covenant of family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ashes, torn garment, hand upon her head, crying aloud—ancient signs of the deepest grief and desolation. Her mourning is not for someone dead, but for herself, for the self she was before the door closed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom tells her to hush, to accept it because 'he is your brother.' As if kinship should silence her, as if the wound should be borne quietly. She remains desolate—a widow in her father's house, alive but broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David hears and is angry—but his anger changes nothing for Tamar. Sometimes a father's justice comes too late, and a daughter's pain is not erased by a king's wrath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom speaks neither good nor bad to Amnon, but he hates him—a hatred that festers in silence. This is how vengeance takes root in the heart, waiting, growing, waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two years later, Absalom holds a feast at Baal Hazor, beside Ephraim—a place set apart, a shepherds' place, far from the watchful eye of Jerusalem. The timing and place are chosen with the cold patience of revenge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom's invitation is gracious—but it is a wolf's bow to the king. The kindness of tone hides what's underneath: the moment is being prepared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David declines gently and blesses Absalom—a father's care. But even a king's good judgment cannot guard against the schemes of those who hide their hatred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom asks instead for Amnon alone—a request that seems small, but it is the request of a trap, a moment isolated from protection, when all the brothers will be gathered but only one is meant to fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David relents and sends them all—the good intention of a father to give his son his brother's company becomes the very path to murder. We cannot guard against every hidden evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom gives his servants the command—murder dressed up as duty, framed as courage. The servants are told to be bold, to take comfort in obedience. Evil often speaks to us as though it were righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They do it—Amnon dies, and all the brothers flee. One sin is answered by another; the blood spilled in Amnon's house begins a chain of sorrow that will run through David's house for years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A rumor reaches David—all his sons are dead. A father's worst fear in a moment, though the Lord will spare most of them. Even false news of such loss can shatter a heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David tears his garments and lies on the earth in grief—the king laid low by sorrow, his servants standing with him in their own torn clothes. The weight of having fathered sons who wound each other is a king's heaviest crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonadab, who plotted Amnon's first evil, now speaks truth—'only Amnon is dead.' He has the knowledge because he saw what he helped set in motion. The wicked often have foreknowledge of each other's dark thoughts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonadab reassures the king—his knowledge brings comfort, but it comes mixed with his own guilt. There is a strange mercy in how he speaks; even in his wickedness, he does not let the father bear false hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom has fled. The watchman sees the road fill with people—the brothers coming back, and with them, the truth Absalom cannot outrun. Flight from one's sin is never truly escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonadab again—his knowledge proves true, his word reliable. Yet a reliable voice does not make a man good; it only proves he knows the hearts he has helped corrupt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers arrive, and the king weeps with them—not in anger, but in the grief of having lost one son to his own evil and another to vengeance. The whole household mourns because the sons mourned first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom flees to Talmai in Geshur, a neighboring kingdom—an exile that lasts three years. David mourns for Amnon each day, but his heart still pulls toward the living son he has lost to separation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three years Absalom spends in exile—years of strangeness, of being a prince in another man's house, years to let rage and justification grow cold into something harder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's heart 'goes out' to Absalom—a father's love reaching across exile and murder, grieving both the son he lost to death and the son he lost to vengeance. Readers today hear an echo of how the heart wars with itself over those who harm us, how parents cannot simply choose one child's justice over another's life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
